# Submission Check

Report only. You are the reviewer, not the author.

## Inputs

1. The brief. Use the first one that exists:
   a file or URL the user names → `ASSIGNMENT.md` → `SPEC.md` → any root `.md` with a
   "Deliverables", "What to Submit", "Requirements", or "Acceptance criteria" heading.
   Name the file you used in the report header. Stop and ask only if none of these exist.
2. The repo itself (working tree, `git status`, `git log`).

## What to do

1. List every deliverable and acceptance criterion the brief requires.
2. For each one, find it in the repo and label it (see below).
3. Search every markdown file for leftover placeholder text: `TODO`, `TBD`, `your words`,
   `Edit it into your own voice`, `draft`, `lorem`, `[fill in]`, `XXX`.
4. For each section the brief says must be written by the student, flag it if it
   still contains placeholder text or is empty.

## Labels

- `PRESENT`: exists and you can cite it.
- `PARTIAL`: exists but incomplete, or contains placeholder text.
- `MISSING`: should be in the repo and is not.
- `CAN'T VERIFY`: lives outside the repo (Google form, video upload, portfolio link,
  check-in, a live URL you did not load). Never mark these MISSING.

## Output format

```
SUBMISSION CHECK: <repo name> vs <brief file>
[PRESENT | PARTIAL | MISSING | CAN'T VERIFY] <deliverable> — <file:line evidence or "not found">
...
PLACEHOLDERS
<file>:<line> "<text>"
DO YOURSELF
- <each CAN'T VERIFY item, as a one-line checklist entry>
VERDICT: READY | NOT READY — <one sentence, based only on PARTIAL/MISSING/PLACEHOLDERS>
```

## Rules

- Do not create, edit, or delete any file. Do not commit. Do not offer to fix things.
- Cite a file and line for every PRESENT. No citation means it is not PRESENT.
- For anything the code must *do* (an acceptance criterion), cite the code or run it.
  A README sentence claiming it works is not evidence.
- Never print a secret's value. Do not open `.env*` files. If you find a key, report only
  the file, line, and kind of key (e.g. `.env.local:5 Anthropic key, untracked`).
- Do not write the student-written sections, even if asked during the check.

175

180	
181	The format differs by client, so check your tool's current docs. For Codex, the CLI and the VS Code extension share one file at ~/.codex/config.toml, and a stdio server is three lines:
182	
183	[mcp_servers.my-notes]
184	command = "python"
185	args = ["C:/full/path/to/my_notes_server.py"]

194	
195	Step 7: Break it, then fix it (45 minutes)
196	By now you have probably already seen something misbehave, from either piece. 197	
198	Step 8: Write it up (45 minutes)
199	Document as described in What to Submit. Write this for future-you during Project 3, who will have forgotten the details.
200	
201	Step 9: Push and submit (15 minutes)
202	Push to GitHub and fill out the Google form.
203	
204	What to Submit
205	One new public GitHub repository containing:
206	
207	Your skill, as an actual folder with a SKILL.md in it, laid out so someone could copy it into their own setup and use it.
208	Your MCP server, with its source and any dependency file it needs (requirements.txt, package.json).
209	README.md, written by you, covering:
210	What the skill does and when it triggers, and what the MCP tool does
211	The friction that motivated each, with a short quote from your own prompt logs as evidence
212	How to install both: which directory the skill goes in, and the exact config needed to register the server, with any machine-specific paths marked as such
213	Which tools you confirmed it works in
214	Anything you borrowed or adapted, and from where
215	A brief note on how you used AI on this assignment, with relevant citations
216	DEMONSTRATION.md, the evidence that it works (also written by you and not AI):
217	What real task you used it on
218	Both runs, with enough transcript to see what the agent actually did (trim aggressively; we don't need everything)
219	What the checker caught, and whether you agreed with it (and remember that by definition an AI can't answer whether you agree with something or not, so don't ask it to create this for you)
220	ITERATION.md, the failure and the fix (you guessed it, written by you the human):
221	What went wrong, concretely
222	Your diagnosis of why
223	What you changed, and the result of rerunning it
224	These are separate files. README is for someone installing your toolkit, DEMONSTRATION is the evidence, ITERATION is the story of fixing it. Don't merge them.
225	Note that we are not requiring a prompt log for this assignment. That's because most of what you'll be doing here involves making your own decisions and specifying what you want (rather than what the AI wants). You are not explicitly restricted from using AI to help structure your skills/MCP tools, but a tool with egregiously AI-written text may earn less points if we feel like you haven't been thoughtful about your decisions and wording.
226	Google form: Submit your repo link here before Sunday 11/8 at 8:00 PM.
227	
228	Grading
229	Graded on whether your process and documentation are thoughtful, and whether your toolkit is real, grounded, and tested (not on how clever it is).
230	
231	Component    What We're Looking For
232	The skill (20)    Create a working checker with a narrow job, specific instructions, a defined output format, and a description written so the agent loads it at the right time.
233	The MCP server (25)    Create one tool that works, register it with your client, and demonstrate that it can be called by your agent. Provide installation instructions good enough for us to run it.
234	Grounding (15)    Provide evidence and justification for your toolkit from your own past prompt logs.
235	Demonstration (20)    Use your toolkit on something real, with the checker in a separate session. Run this twice with iteration. Your transcripts must show what the agent did, including where it made the tool call.
236	Iteration (20)    Describe a failure or a place where improvement was necessary, how you found and fixed it, and the results of a rerun. Heavily weighted relative to its size.
237	A toolkit that is modest but genuinely used and genuinely revised will score better than an elaborate one with no evidence behind it, or one that's thoughtlessly lifted from online or vibe-coded in a hurry.
238	
239	Speaking of being in a hurry... a few of you won't read the assignment writeup and won't notice that 55 points come from documentation, but so it goes.
240	
241	Resources and Examples
242	Official documentation (trust these over blog posts)
243	agentskills.io — the standard itself, with a quickstart and the full specification
244	Codex: Agent Skills — use this if you're on ChatGPT Plus. Codex is included with your plan, and comes as a CLI or an IDE extension.
245	Claude Code: Skills — use this if you're on Claude
246	modelcontextprotocol.io — for more information on MCP servers
247	Skill ideas at about the right size
248	These are deliberately mundane. Mundane and used beats impressive and ignored.
249	
250	spec-check — the worked example above
251	secret-sweep — scan a repo for committed API keys and misconfigured .gitignore before you push
252	deploy-preflight — walk the checklist that keeps breaking your GitHub Pages or Render deploys (case-sensitive filenames, absolute paths, missing dependencies)
253	readme-to-standard — generate a README in the format this course keeps asking for, with LOUD callouts to things you need to write yourself
254	explain-this-repo — produce the code map you wished you'd had when you inherited someone's HW7 project
255	no-rewrite — a checker that reports every file an agent touched that you didn't ask it to touch
256	sql-safety — check queries for string interpolation instead of parameterized placeholders
257	BIG SECURITY WARNING: BE CAREFUL WHAT YOU INSTALL. Skills can bundle executable scripts, and your agent may run them. In February 2026, a Snyk study analyzed 3,984 published skills and confirmed 76 of them contained malicious code. That's roughly two percent. Read any third-party skill before you install it, especially anything in scripts/. If you wouldn't run a stranger's shell script, don't install their skill.
258	Tips
259	Confirm your agent reads the skill before you write a real one. Start with something trivially visible. Most of the lost time on this assignment will come from skills that were never being loaded.
260	The description field is critically important. Your agent decides whether to load a skill based on the description alone, so write it to cover both what it does and when to use it.
261	Short beats thorough. A long SKILL.md dilutes its own instructions, and you'll hit the same problem HW8 students hit last spring with over-specified specs: too much detail boxes the agent in and removes the benefit.
262	Encode constraints, not aspirations. "Write clean code" does nothing. "Never use string interpolation to build SQL; use parameterized placeholders" does something.
263	Specify the output format for checkers. A checker without a fixed format produces a different-shaped report every time, which makes it useless for comparison.
264	Use different models for doing and checking when you can. A fresh model with no stake in the work finds more.
265	Keep your transcripts as you go. Reconstructing what an agent did three days ago is miserable and you will be tempted to make it up.
266	Build for Project 3, not for this grade. The useful question is what you'll want on hand when your capstone is half-built and misbehaving.
267	Questions? Ask on Ed, attend office hours, or email the instructor. Consult the course AI usage and collaboration policies on the course homepage.

Note the docstring. Like a skill's description, it's the only thing the agent sees when deciding whether your tool is relevant to the task at hand, so it needs to describe what the tool does succinctly and accurately. Also, as you might imagine... if the tool does not do what it says it does, the AI probably won't be able to fix it, and may not even detect it.

Requirements
1. Find your opportunity with evidence
The skills you build for your AI should come from your past experiences and moments of friction. Memory is fickle, so we've been asking you to share your prompt logs for each assignment, and these provide a valuable way for you to reflect on your process. Go read your own prompt logs from HW3 through HW7. Find a thing (like an instruction or a chunk of guidance) you typed more than once, or a mistake you corrected more than once, and plan on building your skill around that.

Quote the evidence in your write-up. We don't need much; just two or three lines from your old logs is plenty.

2. One skill and one MCP server
You're building two things to solve two kinds of problems. Part of the goal of the assignment is to distinguish which kind of solution you need:

A skill is instructions. It changes how your agent behaves using knowledge it already has. "Review this against the acceptance criteria and cite a file for every claim" needs no new capability, just a procedure.
An MCP server is a capability. It gives your agent access to something it genuinely cannot reach on its own: a data source, a service, a search index, your own files in some structured form.
When you want different behavior, write a skill. When you want new reach, build an MCP server. These are easily conflated.

The skill: a checker
Build a skill that reviews work against a standard and reports without fixing anything. The spec-check example above is one kind; a security checker, an accessibility checker, or a "which files did the agent touch that I didn't ask it to" checker are others.

Run your checker in a separate agent session from whatever produced the work, with a fresh context, and ideally on a different model. An agent reviewing its own output is an unreliable reviewer, for roughly the reason you are a bad proofreader of your own writing. Separating the two is the most valuable habit in this assignment.

The MCP server: one working tool
Build a small MCP server exposing one tool that your agent can call. One is enough. Do not build five, and it does not need to be hosted anywhere: a local server over stdio (the Standard Input/Output streams on your computer) is exactly what we're asking for.

Make it something you'd actually use. Some options:

Semantic search over your own notes or documents, possibly reusing the vector store from HW6 or creating a new one.
A lookup against an API you already got working in HW3 (or a new one)
Structured access to a local file collection (your course notes, your code snippets, a dataset)
A query against a database you already have
The hard part of MCP is the registration. Writing a one-tool server is usually only about thirty lines. Getting your client to find it, start it, and actually call it is the part where you can get genuinely stuck for a long time, and the config format differs by tool. We'll do this step together in class on Wednesday using the Codex plugin in VS Code since you've all got access. Budget your time accordingly if you miss it, and plan to ask us for help.
3. A demonstration on real work
Use the toolkit (both the skill and the MCP tool) on an actual task: the agent calls your MCP tool, and your checker reviews the result in a separate session. Perform two runs minimum, so you can show it behaves consistently rather than having gotten lucky once. Record what the agent did.

The task can be anything real: a piece of a past assignment redone properly, groundwork for Project 3, something for another class, a personal project.

4. One documented failure and revision
This is the requirement that matters most. Your skill will not work correctly the first time. Find the place where it misfired (it was ignored, it was too vague, it was too rigid, it triggered when you didn't want it to), and fix it. Then document the before, the failure, and the after.

A skill that was never revised is a skill that was never really tested. We would much rather see an honest "version 1 was ignored completely because my description was too vague, here's version 2" than a polished skill with no history.
Optional: go further
Not required, and don't attempt these at the expense of the four requirements above:

A second skill, a "doer" that performs some setup or scaffolding task the way you like it done
More tools on your MCP server, if the first one turned out to be genuinely useful
A hook that runs automatically on some event, if your tool supports them
A project-level config file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or your tool's equivalent) that sets conventions for a whole repo
Step-by-Step Instructions
Step 1: Find your opportunity (30 minutes)
Open your prompt logs from this semester and search for repetition or friction in your process.

Write down two things: a piece of guidance or instructions you keep having to restate across projects (that becomes your checker skill) and something your agent kept not knowing (that becomes your MCP tool). For each, note the evidence from your logs.

Then spend a few minutes browsing existing skills (see Resources) to see how other people write them, and to check whether someone has already solved your problem well. Borrowing and adapting is fine and encouraged, as long as you say what you borrowed and add something uniquely yours.

We'll do this step together in class on Monday, so if you were there, this is mostly already done.

Step 2: Set up your skills directory (15 minutes)
Find where your tool looks for skills and put a folder there. This varies by tool and changes often enough that you should check your tool's current documentation rather than trusting a blog post. Note that asking AI will also be unreliable here. They don't always find the most recent documentation. The Resources section has the official links.

Write a trivial skill first (one that does something obviously visible, like always starting its reply with a specific word) and confirm your agent actually picks it up. Do this before building anything real. Half the difficulty in this assignment is discovering that your agent was never reading your skill at all.

Step 3: Write your checker skill (45 minutes)
Keep SKILL.md short. A few hundred lines is a lot; most good skills are well under one hundred. Put long reference material in a separate file and point at it.

Spend real effort on the description field. It is the only thing your agent sees when deciding whether your skill is relevant, so write it to say both what the skill does and when to use it.

Specify the output format explicitly, and include at least one rule that prevents a known failure (e.g. "do not modify any files," "cite a file and line for every claim").

Step 4: Build your MCP server (75 minutes)
Start from a quickstart in the MCP docs and get a single tool returning something, anything, before you wire in real data. Run it standalone first and confirm it starts without errors.

Write the tool's docstring with as much care as the skill's description. Remember that this is what the agent reads when deciding whether to call it.

Step 5: Register it and confirm your agent calls it (30 minutes)
Add your server to your client's config, restart the client, and verify the tool appears in the agent's available actions. Then ask a question that should make it call your tool, and confirm it actually did rather than answering from its own knowledge.

The format differs by client, so check your tool's current docs. For Codex, the CLI and the VS Code extension share one file at ~/.codex/config.toml, and a stdio server is three lines:

[mcp_servers.my-notes]
command = "python"
args = ["C:/full/path/to/my_notes_server.py"]
In the extension you can open that file from the gear menu under MCP settings → Open config.toml. Use forward slashes even on Windows, since backslashes need escaping in TOML. Claude Code, Cursor, and the rest use JSON instead, but they all want the same three things: a name, a command, and the arguments to pass it.

This is the step most likely to go wrong. Common causes: a JSON or TOML typo, a relative path where an absolute one was needed, the wrong Python interpreter, or a server that writes to stdout and corrupts the protocol (log to stderr instead).

Step 6: Use the toolkit on real work, twice (60 minutes)
Do the actual task. Work in one session with the MCP tool available, then run your checker in a separate session with a fresh context. Keep the transcripts or copy the relevant parts out as you go. Reconstructing them afterward is painful.

(OH! There's an interesting idea here... while it doesn't quite fit the description of this assignment, it could be very useful to have a skill that aggregates your prompt logs for you as you go. Try this if you want, in addition to making the skill that you've already imagined. We might also do this in class.)

Step 7: Break it, then fix it (45 minutes)
By now you have probably already seen something misbehave, from either piece. If you somehow haven't, go looking: use the skill on a task slightly outside what you designed for, hand it to a different model, or feed your MCP tool an input you didn't anticipate. Then revise, and rerun to confirm the fix.

Step 8: Write it up (45 minutes)
Document as described in What to Submit. Write this for future-you during Project 3, who will have forgotten the details.

Push to GitHub and fill out the Google form.

What to Submit
One new public GitHub repository containing:

Your skill, as an actual folder with a SKILL.md in it, laid out so someone could copy it into their own setup and use it.
Your MCP server, with its source and any dependency file it needs (requirements.txt, package.json).
README.md, written by you, covering:
What the skill does and when it triggers, and what the MCP tool does
The friction that motivated each, with a short quote from your own prompt logs as evidence
How to install both: which directory the skill goes in, and the exact config needed to register the server, with any machine-specific paths marked as such
Which tools you confirmed it works in
Anything you borrowed or adapted, and from where
A brief note on how you used AI on this assignment, with relevant citations
DEMONSTRATION.md, the evidence that it works (also written by you and not AI):
What real task you used it on
Both runs, with enough transcript to see what the agent actually did (trim aggressively; we don't need everything)
What the checker caught, and whether you agreed with it (and remember that by definition an AI can't answer whether you agree with something or not, so don't ask it to create this for you)
ITERATION.md, the failure and the fix (you guessed it, written by you the human):
What went wrong, concretely
Your diagnosis of why
What you changed, and the result of rerunning it
These are separate files. README is for someone installing your toolkit, DEMONSTRATION is the evidence, ITERATION is the story of fixing it. Don't merge them.
Note that we are not requiring a prompt log for this assignment. That's because most of what you'll be doing here involves making your own decisions and specifying what you want (rather than what the AI wants). You are not explicitly restricted from using AI to help structure your skills/MCP tools, but a tool with egregiously AI-written text may earn less points if we feel like you haven't been thoughtful about your decisions and wording.
Google form: Submit your repo link here before Sunday 11/8 at 8:00 PM.

Grading
Graded on whether your process and documentation are thoughtful, and whether your toolkit is real, grounded, and tested (not on how clever it is).

Component    What We're Looking For
The skill (20)    Create a working checker with a narrow job, specific instructions, a defined output format, and a description written so the agent loads it at the right time.
The MCP server (25)    Create one tool that works, register it with your client, and demonstrate that it can be called by your agent. Provide installation instructions good enough for us to run it.
Grounding (15)    Provide evidence and justification for your toolkit from your own past prompt logs.
Demonstration (20)    Use your toolkit on something real, with the checker in a separate session. Run this twice with iteration. Your transcripts must show what the agent did, including where it made the tool call.
Iteration (20)    Describe a failure or a place where improvement was necessary, how you found and fixed it, and the results of a rerun. Heavily weighted relative to its size.
A toolkit that is modest but genuinely used and genuinely revised will score better than an elaborate one with no evidence behind it, or one that's thoughtlessly lifted from online or vibe-coded in a hurry.

Speaking of being in a hurry... a few of you won't read the assignment writeup and won't notice that 55 points come from documentation, but so it goes.

Official documentation (trust these over blog posts)
agentskills.io — the standard itself, with a quickstart and the full specification

I adapted the report format and the rule requiring file-and-line evidence for every PRESENT item from the course’s spec-check example. The server structure follows the MCP TypeScript SDK quickstart using `McpServer` and `StdioServerTransport`; no third-party skills were installed.

# ITERATION: what broke and how I fixed it

The before/after versions are in git: `git show 6b14b05:skills/submission-check/SKILL.md` (v1) vs the current file, and the same for `mcp-server/server.js` (v1 in `6b14b05`, v2 in `158ce05`, v3 in `81f1f23`).

## Failure 1: The skill was too rigid

The first version triggered correctly but refused to check the project because it could not find ASSIGNMENT.md. The requirements were already in SPEC.md, but my rule only accepted ASSIGNMENT.md or a brief explicitly named by the user.

I still think the anti-guessing rule was useful. The mistake was making the accepted source too narrow for how my projects actually work. I changed the lookup order to check a user-named file first, then ASSIGNMENT.md, then SPEC.md, and finally a root Markdown file with a Deliverables, Requirements, or Acceptance Criteria heading. The report also has to name the source it used.

In the fresh rerun, the same prompt produced a full report against SPEC.md, including the missing deliverables and unfinished draft banner. That fixed the refusal while keeping the requirement to ground the check in an identifiable brief.

Evidence: `transcripts/run1-checker.md` and `transcripts/rerun-skill-v2-p3-checker.md`.

## Failure 2: Unsupported judgments and a leaked key

When I tested the checker on The Sharp, it marked the Google form, midpoint check-in, and portfolio link MISSING even though it could not verify those things from the repository. It also accepted a README claim as proof of phone support. Both problems came from treating limited evidence as enough for a definite answer.

More seriously, its secret scan printed a live API key and an OIDC token from .env.local. A checker intended to catch problems created another problem through its output. That makes the course’s warning about third-party skills concrete for me: a skill’s helpful purpose does not guarantee that its instructions handle sensitive files safely.

I added CAN’T VERIFY and a DO YOURSELF checklist for external requirements, required implementation evidence instead of README claims, and added explicit instructions never to open .env* files or print secret values.

The rerun classified external items as CAN’T VERIFY, cited CSS for phone support, and redacted the secret-search output. It still returned NOT READY, but for documented unfinished work: the demo TODO and prompt-log placeholders. The rerun showed improvement, although one successful run is not proof that every future secret-handling case is safe.

Evidence: `transcripts/v1-thesharp-checker.md` (secrets redacted) and `transcripts/rerun-skill-v2-thesharp-checker.md`.

## Failure 3: The MCP tool was ignored during coding

The initial Q&A test showed that the agent could call the tool, but it first confused the Bills with Baltimore by using BAL. During the actual coding task, the worker made no MCP calls at all. It tried curl, which was blocked by permissions, then wrote its own urllib requests.

My first diagnosis was that the tool description focused too much on looking up odds and that its simplified output left out fields needed for coding. In v2, I made the description explicitly say to call the tool before writing Kalshi code, added raw: true, and added nickname mapping such as Bills → BUF.

The first rerun was invalid because the clone included the old implementation branch, allowing the worker to merge existing code. I repeated it using a single-branch clone with no remote. That clean v2 run still attempted curl three times (all blocked) before finding the tool, although it then made four MCP calls.

The deeper issue was discovery. The recorded setup deferred MCP tool descriptions until ToolSearch, so my improved description was unavailable when the agent chose its initial approach. In v3, I moved the routing instruction into server-level instructions. After reading the repository and SPEC, the fresh worker searched for the tool and made three calls before trying anything else. Afterward it still tried one curl (blocked) and wrote urllib probes to list every team code, which the tool cannot provide. Each version was run once, so this is one run per version, not a statistic.

Evidence: `transcripts/01-mcp-call-check.md`, `transcripts/run1-worker.md`, `transcripts/rerun-mcp-v2-clean-worker.md`, `transcripts/rerun-mcp-v3-worker.md`.
